lessons.title: How LLMs work
lessons.explain: An LLM predicts the next token given previous ones, learned from massive text. It has no memory between calls — everything it 'knows' about your task must be in the prompt (the context window).
objectives: Explain next-token prediction and why LLMs are stateless between calls

lessons.title: Tokens & tokenization for LLMs
objectives: Explain practical implications of sub-word tokenization for LLM usage
Explain how sub-word tokenization changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect sub-word tokenization with token-based billing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: As covered conceptually in the NLP and Transformers tracks, LLMs process sub-word tokens, not whole words or characters.
examples:
# rough intuition (varies by tokenizer):
# 'the' -> 1 token
# 'photosynthesis' -> maybe 2-3 tokens
# a rare technical term or non-English word -> often even more tokens per word
# -- this is why token counts, not word counts, drive real cost and context budgeting
commonMistakes: Estimating cost or context usage in words instead of tokens — actual token counts can be 30-50% higher than a naive word count, especially for technical or non-English text.
lessons.careerRelevance: Token-budget awareness is a routine, practical daily concern in any real LLM application, directly affecting cost and design decisions.

lessons.title: Instruction tuning & alignment
objectives: Explain how a raw next-token predictor becomes a helpful, instruction-following assistant
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: LoRA / PEFT, QLoRA.
Explain how instruction tuning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect instruction tuning with alignment and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A purely pretrained model (next-token prediction on raw internet text) is good at continuing text patterns, but not necessarily at being a HELPFUL assistant — it might continue a question with more questions rather than answering it.
examples:
# raw pretrained model given 'What is the capital of France?' might continue:
# 'What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Spain?' (just continuing a pattern)
# instruction-tuned model: 'The capital of France is Paris.' (learned to actually ANSWER)
commonMistakes: Assuming 'bigger pretrained model' alone produces a better assistant — instruction tuning and alignment are what actually turn a raw text-continuation engine into something that reliably.
lessons.careerRelevance: This pretrain-then-align pipeline is the standard shape behind every major assistant-style LLM product today. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Inference & decoding: greedy, sampling & temperature
objectives: Explain how a trained LLM turns probabilities into an actual generated response
Explain how greedy decoding changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect greedy decoding with sampling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: At each step, an LLM computes a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary for the next token. Greedy decoding always picks the single highest-probability token (deterministic, but can be repetitive/boring).
examples:
# temperature intuition:
# temperature -> 0: almost always picks the top token (deterministic, focused)
# temperature = 1: samples proportional to the model's real learned probabilities
# temperature > 1: flattens the distribution further, more random/surprising choices
commonMistakes: Using high temperature for tasks needing precise, factual, repeatable output (like structured data extraction) — that's exactly where LOW temperature (or greedy decoding) is the right.
lessons.careerRelevance: Temperature and decoding strategy are among the first practical settings tuned when an LLM application's output is too repetitive or too erratic.

lessons.title: Context windows in practice
objectives: Make practical trade-offs around a model's context window limit
Explain how context budget management changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect context budget management with truncation vs summarization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Building on the Transformers track's explanation of WHY context windows are computationally expensive, this lesson is about the PRACTICAL side: everything you want the model to consider — system instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, the user's question — must fit within one finite token budget, competing with each other.
examples:
# a context budget is a competition for space:
# system prompt (500 tokens) + conversation history (variable) + retrieved docs (variable) + user question
# -- all must fit inside, say, an 8,000 token limit -- something has to be prioritized/trimmed
commonMistakes: Naively appending the full conversation history to every request with no trimming strategy — long conversations will eventually exceed the context limit or silently push out important.
lessons.careerRelevance: Context-budget management is a concrete, daily engineering concern building any real conversational or document-heavy LLM application.

lessons.title: Hallucinations
objectives: Explain why LLMs hallucinate and describe practical mitigation strategies
Explain how hallucination changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect hallucination with fabricated confidence and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: LLMs generate plausible-sounding text based on learned patterns, with no built-in mechanism to verify factual truth — a confident, fluent, completely fabricated citation or statistic is not a rare glitch, it's an expected failure mode of how these models fundamentally work.
examples:
# a hallucination looks EXACTLY as confident and fluent as a correct answer --
# there's no built-in 'uncertainty flag' the model reliably surfaces on its own
# this is precisely the problem RAG (grounding in real retrieved documents) is designed to reduce
commonMistakes: Trusting an LLM's confident tone as a signal of factual accuracy — confidence and correctness are not correlated the way they are in human communication; fluency is not evidence of truth.
lessons.careerRelevance: Hallucination mitigation is one of the most consequential practical design decisions in any real LLM product, directly motivating the RAG track next.

lessons.title: Model evaluation for LLMs
objectives: Describe how LLMs are evaluated, including benchmarks and their limits
Explain how benchmarks changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect benchmarks with application-specific evaluation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: LLMs are evaluated with standardized benchmarks (measuring reasoning, knowledge, coding ability on fixed test sets) AND application-specific evaluation (does THIS model work well for YOUR specific task, on YOUR real data).
examples:
# general benchmarks measure broad capability across many tasks
# but 'best on benchmark X' doesn't guarantee 'best for MY specific customer-support use case'
# -- always evaluate candidates against your OWN representative test set before choosing
commonMistakes: Choosing a model purely by benchmark leaderboard position without testing it on your actual use case — general benchmark performance is a weak proxy for how well a model handles your.
lessons.careerRelevance: Building task-specific evaluation is a real, expected skill for any engineer selecting or comparing LLMs for a product.

lessons.title: Latency, cost & compute
objectives: Reason about the practical trade-offs between model size, latency, and cost
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: LLM API rate limits, retry/backoff for model APIs, token-cost budgeting.
Explain how model size vs cost changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model size vs cost with latency budgets and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Larger models are generally more capable but slower and more expensive per request; smaller models are cheaper and faster but may need more careful prompting or fine-tuning to hit the same quality bar for a narrow task.
examples:
# a customer-support ticket classifier likely doesn't need the largest, most expensive model available --
# a smaller, cheaper, faster model (possibly fine-tuned) may hit the same practical accuracy
# at a fraction of the cost and latency, for this NARROW task
commonMistakes: Defaulting to the largest/most expensive model for every task 'to be safe' — this is often needless cost and latency for tasks a smaller model handles just as well.
lessons.careerRelevance: Cost/latency trade-off reasoning is a routine, expected part of any real production LLM application design discussion. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Safety, responsible use & open vs closed models
objectives: Contrast open and closed model access models, and describe responsible-use basics
Explain how open vs closed models changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect open vs closed models with self-hosting trade-offs and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Closed models (accessed via an API, weights not available) are typically easier to use and stay current, but you depend entirely on the provider for availability, pricing, and policy changes. Open-weight models can be self-hosted, audited, and fine-tuned freely, at the cost of needing your own infrastructure and expertise to run well.
examples:
# closed (API-based): fast to start, provider handles infra, but you don't control the weights or guarantee availability
# open-weight: full control, can self-host and fine-tune freely, but you own the operational burden
commonMistakes: Assuming this choice is purely technical — it also has real business implications (vendor lock-in, cost predictability, data privacy requirements) that should factor into the decision.
lessons.careerRelevance: This trade-off is a common, realistic system-design and architecture-decision discussion point in AI engineering interviews.

The instruction wasn't removed from the conversation history, but the context budget has grown far past what it was earlier. What's the most likely cause, and what's one concrete mitigation?
exercises.hint: the context window likely exceeded the model's effective limit, so the earliest tokens (including that instruction) were truncated or its influence diluted by everything after it -- mitigations include repeating critical instructions closer to the end of the context, summarizing/compacting older history instead of keeping it verbatim, or using a system-level instruction that persists separately from conversation history

description: How models like this one work — tokens, attention, prompting, fine-tuning.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide between an open-source and a closed/API-based model for a given feature?
interviewPreparation.a: Data sensitivity (can this data leave your infrastructure at all), cost structure at your expected volume (per-request API cost vs. self-hosting infrastructure cost), and how much control you need over the model itself (fine-tuning, weight access) all factor in -- there's rarely a universally right answer, only the right tradeoff for this specific feature's constraints.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you choose greedy decoding over sampling with temperature, or vice versa?
interviewPreparation.a: Greedy decoding (or low temperature) gives consistent, repeatable output, which matters for factual extraction or tasks needing the same answer every time. Higher temperature sampling introduces controlled randomness, useful for creative tasks where varied, less predictable output is actually desirable, not a defect.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you manage context as a conversation grows beyond what comfortably fits in the context window?
interviewPreparation.a: Options include truncating older history, summarizing it instead of keeping it verbatim, or using retrieval to pull back only what's relevant rather than keeping everything -- the right choice depends on whether older context is still likely to matter, and whether losing some fidelity is an acceptable tradeoff for staying within budget.

interviewPreparation.q: What would a good task-specific evaluation plan for an LLM feature actually include?
interviewPreparation.a: A real test set representative of what the feature will actually see in production, and explicit scoring criteria tied to what matters for this specific task -- not just running it against a generic benchmark, which may not reflect the feature's actual failure modes or success criteria at all.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you mitigate the risk of a model hallucinating in a specific feature, beyond a generic disclaimer?
interviewPreparation.a: Grounding the model's response in retrieved, verifiable source material (rather than relying purely on its internal knowledge) when factual accuracy matters, and being explicit in the interface about what's model-generated versus sourced -- a disclaimer alone doesn't reduce the actual rate of fabricated claims, it just describes the risk.

careerApplications: Directly relevant if targeting AI-focused roles (e.g. ByteDance AI teams).

capstone.title: Build and defend a production-minded LLM feature, not just a working prompt
capstone.description: Take a real LLM-powered feature idea and design it the way it would actually need to work in production: a justified model choice (open vs. closed, size vs. cost), a decoding strategy matched to the task, an explicit strategy for managing context budget as conversations grow, a task-specific evaluation plan (not just 'it seems to work'), and a documented mitigation for at least one hallucination risk specific to this feature. This is about the judgment layer around an LLM, not prompt-writing alone -- the same judgment a team would actually need before shipping this to real users.
deliverables: A specific LLM feature idea with a justified model choice (open vs. closed, and roughly what size/cost tier) tied to the feature's actual latency and cost constraints
A decoding strategy (temperature, sampling vs. greedy) chosen and justified for this specific task, not a default
An explicit context-budget strategy for how the feature behaves as input grows (truncation, summarization, or retrieval), not an assumption that everything always fits
A task-specific evaluation plan: a real test set and scoring criteria for this feature specifically, not a generic benchmark
A documented hallucination risk specific to this feature and a concrete mitigation, not a generic disclaimer
capstone.portfolioTips: The task-specific evaluation plan is the piece most people skip, and it's exactly what makes this look like real production judgment rather than a prompt-engineering demo -- a reviewer who sees a real test set and scoring criteria knows you've thought past 'it worked when I tried it.'

industryUsage.usage: Publishes extensive guidance on decoding parameters, evaluation, and hallucination mitigation, since these are exactly the practical decisions that determine whether an LLM feature is actually reliable in production.
Emphasizes task-specific evaluation and explicit context-management strategy as core parts of building reliable LLM-powered products, not implementation details left to chance.
Operating LLM features at massive scale makes model right-sizing (cost/latency tradeoffs) and context-budget management direct, measurable engineering and cost decisions, not academic considerations.
